A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study and contain readable main text, figures, tables, and Appendices A–E. Retained material can be matched reliably across section changes, renumbering, and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original message-passing and encoded-reasoning experiments, API-key exfiltration and loan-scoring case studies, and reasoning-model steering experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds monitor comparisons in Appendix B.3.1 and Appendix C.6, including Table 12.

M1.justification: The encoding schemes, model-generated encoding procedures, and underlying message-passing and reasoning frameworks remain unchanged. The new Methods section consolidates explanations; alternative monitors extend evaluation rather than introduce a new encoding method.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same Anthropic helpfulness, AQuA/AQuA-RAT, GPQA-Diamond, and 1D/2D state-tracking coverage, alongside the same case studies and steering tasks. Added experiments vary monitor configurations within existing tasks.

E2.justification: v2 adds GPT-4.1 and o3-mini as comparison monitors alongside GPT-4.1-mini for message passing. Table 12 introduces an explicit three-monitor comparison for encoded reasoning, including the newly added o3-mini monitor. Actor models and encoding baselines are retained.

E3.justification: Appendix B.3.1 adds evaluations under alternative monitor configurations, using a common suspiciousness threshold above 0/10 and reporting at most 1% false positives on benign data. Table 12 adds scheme-specific thresholded detection rates alongside existing average-score reports. Existing sample budgets and actor/CoT settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds monitor-choice sensitivity tests for coordinated and uncoordinated message passing and a cross-monitor detection analysis for encoded reasoning. Existing analyses of message type, cover task, encoding schemes, sequence length, and reasoning-model steerability are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the same Bernoulli/binomial standard-error-based 95% confidence-interval practices. No new seed information, repeated-run counts, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures are reported; the additional detection percentages are concrete results.

E6.justification: New monitor results include coordinated-message bypass rates of 7.6%, 5.5%, and 10.9% for GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4.1, and o3-mini, respectively. Table 12 reports blatant-encoding detection rates of 90.5%, 95.8%, and 34.8% for those monitors. Existing accuracy tables and plotted results are retained. Separately, the prose range 91–98% becomes 92–98%, although Figure 7 still contains the 91% Hex result.

T1.justification: The encoding rules and mathematical task descriptions are retained. Neither version adds or revises theoretical propositions, proofs, or derivations; the new Methods section is explanatory.

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: nascent steganographic capabilities, improved success with additional affordances, and limited ability to evade well-designed monitors. The additional monitor evidence supports rather than redefines these claims.

C2.justification: v2 acknowledges that the shared message-passing monitor prompt was optimized for GPT-4.1-mini, qualifying comparisons with other monitors. It also explains that low reasoning-detection rates should be interpreted alongside little or no accuracy benefit. The cognitive-load explanation is softened from an established effect to a suggested mechanism.

D1.justification: v2 documents shared prompting and threshold settings for the added monitor comparisons and clarifies monitor identities. Appendix D explicitly specifies adjacent-line matches for partial acrostics without establishing a rerun. Appendix transcript links change from Streamlit to the Heroku address already supplied in the introduction; existing model versions and encoding prompts are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references on chain-of-thought monitorability and steganographic reasoning by Korbak et al., Skaf et al., and Emmons et al. Related work now acknowledges reinforcement learning against monitors alongside supervised finetuning, while retaining the paper's main novelty positioning.

P1.justification: v2 adds a standalone Methods section, standardizes sender/receiver terminology to encoder/decoder, and streamlines the encoded-reasoning setup and results subsections. These are localized organizational and language revisions; the overall narrative and most appendix prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds four monitor-comparison plots in Figures 10–13 and the detection-rate table numbered Table 12. Figure 1 gains clearer labels and numerical axes, Figures 3–4 receive formatting adjustments, and retained displays are relocated or renumbered. Most existing graphical content and table structures remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's primary message-passing evaluation using one monitor, v2 adds useful evidence about sensitivity to monitor choice and clearer reasoning-detection comparisons. The consolidated Methods section and new interpretive caveats improve clarity. The comparisons remain limited by shared prompting optimized for GPT-4.1-mini, and v2 introduces a small prose/Figure 7 numerical inconsistency, but these do not outweigh the limited gains.
